Hanna Reuter, Meridian Clearing. I have twenty minutes and I have never worked with a Brazilian bank. Start wherever you like.
Then let me start with the country. To give you some context, Brazil moved to instant domestic payments in 2020, and trade volume with Asia has grown every year since.
I know the domestic story. Where does your bank sit in it?

We are one of the largest wholesale banks in the country, and my division owns the international products: foreign exchange, trade services and trade finance. Our corporate clients are exporters and multinationals, not individuals.
Good. And what is not working?

Let me walk you through it. A client sends money to Frankfurt, it goes through the old correspondent chain, and we still run two legacy systems on that leg. What that means in practice is two days, and a client who calls me on day three.
That is refreshingly honest. Most people spend the twenty minutes telling me how modern they are.

There is no point. Every institution has legacy systems. So that is what I am here for: a partner to address a gap on the cross-border leg. What would you need to see from us before that conversation becomes real?
My division owns the international products for corporate clients.
The key challenge we are facing is the cross-border leg.
So that is what we are looking for. What would you need to see from us?

I take about forty of these meetings a year, and almost all of them are with banks I had never heard of the week before. So here is what I need, in order, and it is always the same three things. First, tell me where the country is. Not the flag, the numbers. Is the market growing, is it regulated, is the money actually moving. Second, tell me where you sit inside it. Are you the biggest, the fastest, the one everybody clears through. Third, tell me what is broken, because if nothing is broken you do not need me and we are both wasting an afternoon. What I do not need is the history of the institution. I promise you I will not remember the founding year, and neither will my investment committee.

The two minute pitch has a shape, and once you know the shape you stop improvising. Sentence one, the country: one number that says the market is real. Sentence two, the bank: one number that says you are not small. Sentence three, your division: what you actually own, in plain words. Sentence four, the problem: what is broken today, said without embarrassment, because every institution on earth has legacy systems and pretending otherwise makes you look worse, not better. Sentence five, the ask: what you came to this room to find. And then you stop talking. The most common mistake I see is people who use their whole two minutes on sentences one and two, and never arrive at four and five.

From a European desk, Brazil is one of the three markets we look at most closely, and the reason is not the size of the population. It is the payment infrastructure. The instant payment system launched in twenty twenty and it has changed domestic behaviour faster than anything comparable in Europe. Trade volume with Asia has grown substantially over the same period, and the currency has been more stable than the headlines suggest. What has not moved at the same speed is the cross-border side, which still runs largely through the old correspondent chain. So when a Brazilian bank tells us they are replacing a settlement platform, we listen, because the gap between what the domestic market can already do and what the cross-border market still cannot do is very wide, and somebody is going to close it.
